new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and non-contrastive: it falls on the first syllable of the (root of the) word; inflectional and derivational suffixes are unstressed and never shift it. Independently confirmed by Bodt 2014: 422 ('Stress in general is non-distinctive... In both disyllabic and polysyllabic words, stress falls on the first syllable. This also holds for polymorphemic lexemes') and for the Bjokapakha variety by Grollmann 2020: 50 ('trochaic pattern... stress lies on the first syllable... In words with more than two syllables, stress falls also on the first syllable').
new_statements.secondary_stress: No 'secondary stress' term seen in the snippets. Compounds keep the stress of each component: Andvik 2010 (2.4 'Stress on compounds') 'Compounds composed of a disyllabic followed by a monosyllabic lexeme are stressed on first and third syllable' (doma-pan 'beetlenut', lanyi-ngam 'moon', kewa-nong 'birthday'); Grollmann 2020: 50 'stress lies on the first syllab[l]e of each component'.
new_statements.exceptions: Andvik 2010: 19-20: for the few monomorphemic lexemes of more than two syllables 'the syllable structure may determine stress placement, with stress attracted to a closed (VC or CVC) syllable, although more research is needed on this. Trisyllabic forms with an open (CV) second syllable take initial stress: dazere, tukuli, anyimo, baktulup...' whereas forms like meaktsa 'wife', pheaktsa 'husband', balingmi 'white', morenmo 'widow', lasokpa, galakpa have 'stress on the second syllable'; non-derived tetrasyllables rare. Bodt 2014: 422 notes 'some exceptions among compound[s]', e.g. samtoka [samˈtoːkaː] 'otter', nasbaktang, and marks stress in his lexicon only 'whenever it is not predictable'. Loans from Dzongkha/Tibetan not seen discussed in snippets.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation/lexical words; rule stated relative to the root (affixes are suffixal and unstressed; behaviour with the negative prefix ma- not visible in the snippets). Variety: Trashigang (E Bhutan) Tshangla. Bodt adds stress is 'relatively unpronounced' phonetically; the Pemakö (Tibet) variety is reported to be developing tone instead (Andvik 2003: 439-40).
new_statements.identity_note: Andvik 2010 describes the Trashigang-district (eastern Bhutan) variety, i.e. standard Tshangla = tsha1245. Bodt 2014 is a pan-dialectal phonology (Bhutan, Dirang/Arunachal, Pemakö/Tibet) and agrees. Grollmann 2020 describes Bjokapakha, a divergent Tshangla variety of Bjoka (Zhemgang, central Bhutan), filed under tsha1245 in Glottolog 5.1's bibliography (no separate glottocode known); it shows the same initial (trochaic) stress. The Pemakö/Metog variety (Cangluo Menba, Zhang 1986) is reported to be developing a tone contrast (Andvik 2003: 439-440) and was not checked for stress.
